new_statements.translation: In Maxakalí, lexical stress is predictable: it falls, in most cases, on the last syllable of the phonological word. It is dynamic, i.e. the pitch, intensity and duration of stressed syllables are in general higher than those of unstressed syllables. The examples in (50) below show various morphophonological contexts indicating that stress in Maxakalí falls on the last syllable of the word. [...] Compounds (50i-j) again receive stress on the last syllable. Stress also falls on clitics postposed to pronominal (50k-l), verbal (50m) and nominalized (50n) roots.
new_statements.citation: Silva, Mário André Coelho da. 2020. Tikmũũn yĩy ax tinã xohi xi xahĩnãg – Sons e pedaços da língua Maxakalí: descrição da fonologia e morfologia de uma língua Macro-Jê. Tese de Doutorado, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, printed p. 123 = PDF p. 124 (extracted text verified), §2.6 'Acento lexical' opens exactly: 'No Maxakalí, o acento lexical é previsível: ele incide, na maior parte dos casos, na última sílaba da palavra fonológica. Ele tem caráter dinâmico, isto é, o pitch, intensidade e duração de sílabas acentuadas são, em geral, mais elevados que o de sílabas não acentuadas. Os exemplos em (50) abaixo mostram... recai sobre a última sílaba da palavra.' and, after the elided sentences on (50a-h), 'Compostos, exemplificados em (50i-j), recebem o acento, novamente, na última sílaba. O acento também recai em clíticos pospostos a raízes pronominais (50k-l), verbais (50m) e nominalizadas (50n).'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (roots, prefixed roots, compounds, and root+enclitic strings alike); phonetic echo vowels produced by coda lenition are not phonological syllables and never bear stress. Independently confirmed by Campos 2009 p. 23: 'Com relação ao acento, este localiza-se, normalmente, na última sílaba em Maxakalí.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Silva 2020 says nothing about secondary stress; he reports (p. 53) that Popovich & Popovich 1960b claimed compounds carry one stress per member, whereas his own data show compounds with a single final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Diminutive suffix /-dãk/ does not attract stress: stress stays on the last syllable of the base (verbs and nouns), shown by pitch/intensity and by emphatic lengthening of the base vowel; (ii) lexicalized /-cɛkka/ 'big' has initial stress for elderly speakers (old root+suffix), regularized to final stress /-cɛka/ [ʨɛˈka] by younger adults; (iii) a handful of vowel-sequence items (e.g. /bai/ 'good', /daik/ 'pot', loan /cabaũk/ 'soap') sound penultimate in normal tempo but final in careful elicitation, unresolved; (iv) Portuguese loans keep the Portuguese tonic and delete post-tonic material, so they surface oxytone (two exceptions mesa > [mɛ̃ːˈʥa], moça > [mũːˈʨa], which shift stress to the final).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including enclitics (case, TAM, nominalizer clitics receive the stress). Correlates: pitch, intensity, duration; Silva notes pitch may be intonational since data were elicited isolated words (citing Silva 2011, Popovich 1985 on global declination). Emphatic vowel lengthening targets the stressed vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Both theses describe contemporary spoken Maxakalí (Tikmũũn yĩy ax) of the Terra Indígena Maxakalí, NE Minas Gerais (Água Boa, Pradinho, Aldeia Verde, Cachoeirinha) = Glottolog maxa1247, ISO mbl. Silva 2020 distinguishes it from the ritual-song register (Língua dos Cantos Rituais) and from extinct relatives (Pataxó-Hãhãhãe, Malalí), which are not the object of the stress statement.
